rationale: 256 is not a valid octet, so this is not an IP address and must produce no span.
phileas currently returns [4,12) '56.1.1.1', salvaging an invalid address into a valid-looking match by starting partway through the digits. See philterd/phileas#336.
Every octet is out of range, so there is nothing to match.
256 is not a valid octet, so the text is not an IP address and must produce no span, whichever position the invalid octet is in.

The companion case ip-address/negative-octet-out-of-range covers the leading position. This covers the trailing one, where an implementation that stops the last octet after two digits would report a valid-looking '1.1.1.25' and leave a stray '6' in the output.
A dotted number whose final group runs to five digits is a build or version identifier, not an IP address, so it must produce no span.
The address must not end partway through a longer run of digits: reporting '10.0.0.190' here would redact part of a version string and leave the rest in the clear.
400 exceeds the 0 to 255 octet range, so there is no IP address here and no span may be produced.

Distinct from a value just past the boundary such as 256: 400 fails every octet alternative at its first two digits, so an implementation that matches greedily without a right-hand boundary reports '1.2.3.40'.
